opus-5.5.text:
Oh, Fanfou. That really takes me back. I was a student when I started using it, and I think I was a pretty heavy user. I'd post several times a day and refresh constantly to see what everyone else was saying.

Looking back, it was a very special moment. The Chinese internet was growing incredibly fast, but it still felt small and kind of intimate. The people on Fanfou were early adopters: engineers, writers, people who were curious about everything. You'd follow someone because they said something interesting, not because they were famous. There was no algorithm deciding what you saw. It was just a timeline of people thinking out loud.

For me it was a window into how other people think. As a student you're mostly inside your own little world of coursework and exams. On Fanfou you'd suddenly see a product manager complaining about a launch, someone translating a paper they liked, someone posting a half-formed idea at 2 a.m. I think that shaped me more than I realized at the time. It taught me that ideas don't have to be polished before you share them, and that a lot of value comes from conversations among people who are just genuinely interested.

There's some nostalgia too, because that kind of open, slightly chaotic, low-stakes space is harder to find now. Platforms got bigger and more optimized, and naturally more performative. People are more careful. On Fanfou you could be a bit silly and nobody cared.

Funnily enough, I see some parallels with the research community. In the early days of deep learning, it also felt like a small group of people excitedly sharing things on Twitter or arXiv, everyone talking to everyone. As a field grows, you lose some of that intimacy. So I guess Fanfou left me with an appreciation for those early, messy phases of any community, when things are still being figured out and anyone can jump in and contribute.

fable-5.1.text:
Looking back, it was really a period of discovering that I enjoyed thinking out loud in public. I started using Fanfou around 2007, 2008, when I was still an undergraduate at Shanghai Jiao Tong. It was China's Twitter before Weibo existed, and it was small and strange and full of people who were genuinely curious about things. I'd post constantly, dozens of times a day sometimes, about what I was reading, about computer science, about random observations. Nobody cared about followers then. It felt more like a shared notebook than a platform.

I think what that period gave me was a habit I still have, which is writing down half-formed ideas before they're ready. A lot of research taste comes from being willing to say something slightly wrong in front of other people and then getting corrected. Fanfou was a very low-stakes place to practice that. The community was tiny but surprisingly deep, a lot of early engineers, writers, people who later ended up at Douban or building their own companies.

The other thing I remember is how fast everything moved. The whole Chinese internet was exploding at once, and you could feel that you were watching infrastructure being invented in real time. Then Fanfou got shut down in 2009, and when it came back the moment had passed. That was my first lesson that platforms are temporary but the people and the habits you form on them aren't. A lot of the friends I made there, I'm still in touch with, and some of them I ended up working with later.

So I don't really look at it with nostalgia as much as gratitude. It taught me to be curious in public, and that turned out to matter a lot more than the tool itself.

astra-6.text:
Looking back, I think what mattered was the feeling that you could put a thought out there and it might lead to a conversation you hadn’t expected. I spent a lot of time on Fanfou, and in that period when the internet was growing so quickly, there was always something new to react to, someone new to learn from.

Of course, being a heavy user also meant giving it a lot of attention. Posting frequently isn’t necessarily the same as thinking deeply. But it leaves a record of how you saw things at the time. Looking back at that younger version of yourself can be a little embarrassing, but it also reminds you that your views can change. I think that’s a valuable thing to hold on to.

sol-6.1.text:
Looking back, Fanfou was a place where I could think out loud. I could write down a small observation or a half-formed idea without turning it into a polished essay. And through those everyday posts, you gradually got a sense of how other people thought. That was a very appealing way to connect.

The internet was growing so quickly then that it felt like there was always something new to discover. But what stayed with me was less the speed of that growth than the feeling of curiosity—the possibility that someone outside your immediate circle could introduce you to a completely different perspective. Looking back at what I wrote, I’d probably cringe at some of it. But that’s also part of the value: you leave a record of yourself learning and changing.
